chunks: Types of PCB test points. The question: What are different types of test points?
Test points come in a few common styles, and the right one depends on who will measure and how fast the signal is.

The main styles are a flat surface pad, a through-hole loop or post, an exposed via (a small plated hole), a header or connector, and a coaxial connector (a shielded plug, like a TV cable's) for radio signals.
Each trades space, ease of use and effect on the signal.
Think of the ways to grab something: a flat tab you tap with a tool, a hook you can clip onto, a hole you slip a probe into, or a proper plug.
A factory machine wants a flat tab it can land on from below. A bench engineer wants a hook for a measuring clip. A radio signal wants a plug that does not disturb it.
The analogy has one limit: here every choice also loads the signal a little.
From left to right, a flat SMD pad, a through-hole loop, an exposed via and an RF coax connector. Notice how much height and area each takes and which side of the board it needs.
SMD pad: a flat copper pad on the surface, about 1 mm across, left uncovered by the board's green protective coating (solder mask).
Through-hole loop or post: a wire loop or pin soldered into a hole, easy to clip onto. Via test point: an exposed via used as a pad, saving space.
Header: a row of pins for programming or debug. Bed-of-nails fixture: factory spring pins that land on pads.
One board has four needs. A factory fixture needs flat pads about 1 mm wide, spaced at least 1. 27 mm apart.
The power rail gets a through-hole loop, so an engineer can clip an oscilloscope probe on it. A crowded corner uses an exposed via, which must not be covered or filled.
A fast radio signal gets a tiny pad or a coaxial connector. That is the whole idea.

"The main styles are SMD pads, which are small and fixture-friendly; through-hole loops or posts, which are easy to clip a scope onto; exposed vias for tight boards; headers and connectors for programming and debug; and RF connectors like SMA or U.
FL for high-speed signals. I pick by who measures it, a fixture, an engineer or a technician, and by how fast and sensitive the net is."
